paragraphs: The paper studies how to choose influential starting points in a social network when decisions happen sequentially. After selecting a node, the decision maker sees only which immediate neighbors it activates. Later choices can use this feedback, but they cannot observe the full cascade through the network. The objective is to maximize expected total activation under the independent cascade model.

The authors bound the advantage of adapting decisions to this limited feedback. The largest possible ratio between optimal adaptive and optimal fixed selections lies between e/(e−1) and 4. They also establish constant approximation guarantees for both adaptive and non-adaptive greedy selection, measured against the optimal adaptive strategy.

A notable worst-case result is that non-adaptive greedy has an approximation ratio no worse than adaptive greedy when considering all graphs. This does not say adaptation never helps on a particular network. It establishes the conjectured constant guarantee for adaptive greedy while suggesting that immediate-neighbor feedback may offer relatively limited benefits to that algorithm.
neurips-2019-adaptive-influence-maximiza.tldr: The paper bounds the value of adapting influence-maximization decisions when feedback reveals only a seed’s immediate activations.

paragraphs: A vision model can encounter an image that has been rotated or scaled without its underlying content changing. Certifying robustness means establishing that specified changes cannot undermine the model’s prediction. The paper addresses geometric transformations, which are poorly served by certification methods focused on bounded changes to individual pixel values.

The proposed method combines sampling with optimization to construct linear relaxations of compositions of transformations. These relaxations provide a simpler mathematical description that safely covers the transformations being analyzed. The authors establish soundness and asymptotic optimality: the bounds remain valid, and their approximation quality has an optimal limiting behavior. Asymptotic optimality is a limiting guarantee, rather than a claim that every finite computation is exact.

The implementation, DeepG, certifies substantially more complex geometric transformations than existing methods in the reported evaluation. It works with both defended and undefended networks and scales to large architectures. The contribution is therefore a way to obtain formal guarantees for richer geometric changes, extending the range of transformations that robustness certification can address.
neurips-2019-certifying-geometric-robust.tldr: DeepG combines sampling and optimization to certify neural-network robustness against complex compositions of geometric transformations.

paragraphs: A generative model’s likelihood indicates how compactly data could theoretically be encoded without losing information. Higher probability corresponds to a shorter ideal description. However, knowing that a short code exists does not automatically provide an efficient procedure for encoding and decoding it. This creates a gap between strong probability models and practical compression systems.

The paper targets that gap for flow models. Efficient coding methods were already available for autoregressive models and variational autoencoders, but a corresponding approach was missing for general types of flows. The authors introduce local bits-back coding and develop efficient implementations for many popular flow families. The coding algorithm is thus an essential part of turning the model’s probability estimates into compressed data.

Experiments on high-dimensional data show that these algorithms produce code lengths close to the theoretical lengths of state-of-the-art flow models. This result connects likelihood quality to realizable lossless compression. The stated contribution covers many popular flow types, without claiming an efficient coding solution for every conceivable flow architecture.
neurips-2019-compression-with-flows-via-.tldr: Local bits-back coding turns many flow models into efficient lossless compressors with code lengths close to their theoretical targets.

paragraphs: This paper searches for image classifiers that fit strict memory and execution-time budgets on small computing devices. Its narrow search space focuses on networks suitable for near-sensor Internet-of-Things platforms. Hardware requirements shape the search objective, so the desired result is an accurate model that can actually execute within the device’s constraints.

The approach produces classification latencies below 10 milliseconds on a low-cost device with 1 GB of RAM and 5.6 GFLOPS peak performance. On CIFAR10, searching floating-point architectures raises an established IoT model’s accuracy from 70.64% to 74.87% under the same memory constraints. Including 16-bit formats raises accuracy to 82.07%, and model-optimized reduced IEEE 754 formats reach 83.45%.

The empirical study includes more than 3,000 trained models using reduced precision. Its central finding is that architecture and numerical format can be searched together to improve the accuracy achievable within a memory budget. The reported gains move the observed tradeoff frontier, showing that precision choices can materially affect which network designs are feasible and effective.
neurips-2019-constrained-deep-neural-net.tldr: A constrained architecture search jointly explores network designs and numerical precision to improve image classification within small-device budgets.

paragraphs: DFNets is a convolutional neural-network model for data organized as a graph. Its central component is a class of spectral graph filters with feedback loops. These filters aim to localize processing more effectively around graph vertices while retaining fast convergence and memory requirements that grow linearly.

The paper supplies theoretical support for the filtering procedure. Feedback-looped filters can converge to a specified error bound and can be applied to any graph without advance knowledge of its structure. The model’s propagation rule also diversifies features inherited from earlier layers, which the authors connect to strong gradient flows. Together, these properties address how graph information is processed and how the network can be trained.

The evaluation covers semi-supervised document classification on citation networks and entity classification on a knowledge graph. Across all datasets in those two benchmark tasks, the authors report considerable improvements over state-of-the-art methods. The results support feedback-looped filtering as an effective design in these settings, alongside the separate theoretical guarantees about filter convergence and applicability.
neurips-2019-dfnets-spectral-cnns-for-gr.tldr: DFNets uses feedback-looped graph filters to improve feature localization and training, with strong reported results on two classification benchmarks.

paragraphs: Linear regression is often applied to sensitive information about people. Differential privacy allows statistics to be released with individual privacy guarantees, but the privacy mechanism introduces noise. This paper asks how Bayesian regression should quantify uncertainty when those noisy statistics are the information available for inference.

The distinction matters because a point estimate and a posterior distribution answer different questions. A coefficient estimate summarizes a relationship, while a posterior also expresses uncertainty about that relationship. The authors show that a naive procedure which ignores the added privacy noise performs poorly in realistic data settings. Treating the released statistics as if they were unperturbed fails to account properly for the information available.

The proposed methods explicitly incorporate the privacy mechanism into inference. They account for its noise when constructing posterior distributions and produce correct posteriors across a wide range of scenarios. The contribution is a way to make Bayesian uncertainty assessment reflect the process that generated the private release, extending the focus beyond privately estimating regression coefficients alone.
neurips-2019-differentially-private-baye.tldr: Noise-aware Bayesian regression accounts for the privacy mechanism to quantify uncertainty correctly from privately released statistics.

paragraphs: The paper studies language learning from a continuing stream of text without labels identifying which dataset each example belongs to. In this setting, a model must absorb new examples while retaining useful knowledge from earlier ones. The central problem is catastrophic forgetting: learning new material can damage performance on previously learned material.

The proposed model uses an episodic memory with two mechanisms, sparse experience replay and local adaptation. Replay brings stored experiences back into learning, while local adaptation provides another way to use memory as the model encounters examples. Experiments on text classification and question answering show complementary benefits from the two mechanisms, supporting their combination for continued learning across datasets.

The authors also examine how much memory the approach needs. Randomly selecting which examples to retain reduces the memory module’s space complexity by approximately 50–90%, with only a minimal performance decrease in the reported experiments. This makes the memory component less costly while preserving much of its benefit. The authors position episodic memory as a step toward broader linguistic intelligence, rather than claiming that goal is achieved.
neurips-2019-episodic-memory-in-lifelong.tldr: An episodic memory combines sparse replay and local adaptation to reduce forgetting during continuous language learning without dataset identifiers.

paragraphs: FastSpeech addresses three problems in neural text-to-speech systems: slow generation, skipped or repeated words, and limited control over speaking speed. Many systems first turn text into a mel-spectrogram, a representation used to synthesize audio. FastSpeech accelerates this stage with a feed-forward Transformer that generates the spectrogram in parallel.

Parallel generation requires matching the length of the phoneme sequence to the longer sequence of spectrogram frames. The model learns phoneme durations using alignments extracted from an encoder-decoder teacher. A length regulator then expands the phoneme sequence according to those durations. This gives the model an explicit way to organize timing and adjust speaking speed.

On LJSpeech, the authors report speech quality matching autoregressive models, near elimination of skipped and repeated words in particularly difficult cases, and smooth speed adjustment. Relative to autoregressive Transformer TTS, spectrogram generation is 270 times faster and complete speech synthesis is 38 times faster. The different speedups distinguish acceleration of one processing stage from acceleration of the entire synthesis pipeline.
neurips-2019-fastspeech-fast-robust-and-.tldr: FastSpeech uses predicted phoneme durations and parallel spectrogram generation to accelerate speech synthesis while improving reliability and speed control.

paragraphs: Predicting future video frames requires a model to represent the many ways a scene can evolve over time. Earlier approaches built detailed assumptions into their architectures through components such as optical flow, segmentation masks, and foreground-background separation. This paper asks how much of that specialized machinery is necessary for strong video prediction.

The authors investigate a different design strategy: minimize handcrafted inductive biases while increasing network capacity. The models are large stochastic recurrent neural networks, and the study focuses on whether this general approach can learn effective video dynamics. The empirical question is therefore about the tradeoff between architectural specialization and the capacity of the learned model.

The large-scale study reports state-of-the-art performance on three datasets covering object interactions, human motion, and car driving. These results show that the proposed strategy can work across several distinct kinds of temporal behavior. They provide evidence for large, less specialized models as a viable route to high-quality video prediction, without establishing that handcrafted structure is unnecessary in every video setting.
neurips-2019-high-fidelity-video-predict.tldr: Large stochastic recurrent models achieve strong video prediction across three domains while minimizing handcrafted architectural assumptions.

paragraphs: Cooperative multi-agent learning often trains agents centrally but requires them to act independently during execution. This arrangement accommodates communication constraints while making training manageable. The paper analyzes value-based methods in this setting, concentrating on QMIX and the restrictions it places on representing the value of joint actions.

The authors show that these representation constraints can lead to provably poor exploration and suboptimal behavior. MAVEN addresses the problem by combining value-based agents with a policy that controls a shared latent variable. Each agent conditions its behavior on that variable, creating a higher-level means of directing the team’s exploration.

This shared control enables exploration that remains committed over extended periods, so coordinated behavior can persist across multiple decisions. The paper identifies this capability as important for difficult multi-agent tasks. Experiments report significant performance improvements on SMAC. The contribution connects a theoretical diagnosis of exploration problems in constrained value representations to an architecture designed to support more sustained, coordinated exploration.
neurips-2019-maven-multi-agent-variation.tldr: MAVEN uses a shared latent variable to guide sustained team exploration and address weaknesses in constrained multi-agent value methods.

paragraphs: The paper introduces maximum expected hitting cost, or MEHC, as a measure of difficulty for Markov decision processes. It refines the related diameter measure by incorporating reward structure. This matters because the rewards available while moving through a decision process can affect how informative the learning problem is.

The authors show that MEHC can replace diameter in an upper bound on the optimal value span of an extended decision process. This replacement tightens associated regret bounds for several algorithms resembling UCRL2. The result improves theoretical descriptions of learning difficulty by accounting for rewards alongside the process’s state-transition structure.

The paper also examines potential-based reward shaping, which can produce equivalent reward functions with different informativeness as measured by MEHC. Its analysis formalizes effects on regret and sample complexity in the undiscounted average-reward setting. For a large class of processes with finite MEHC and unsaturated optimal average rewards, shaping changes MEHC by at most a factor of two in either direction. That bound is conditional on the stated class.
neurips-2019-maximum-expected-hitting-co.tldr: MEHC incorporates rewards into decision-process complexity, refining regret bounds and quantifying how reward shaping can change learning difficulty.

paragraphs: Quantization replaces full-precision network weights with discrete values to reduce model size and energy consumption. Training these compressed networks is difficult because the conversion is non-differentiable. The gradients needed to update the underlying weights are therefore unusable directly, motivating approximations such as straight-through estimators and manually designed gradient rules.

MetaQuant learns the update information with a second neural network. This meta network receives the full-precision weights and the gradients with respect to their quantized versions. It outputs gradients for updating the full-precision weights, and it is trained jointly with the quantized network. The method thus makes the gradient approximation itself part of the learning process.

The authors report faster convergence and better performance across experiments on CIFAR10, CIFAR100, and ImageNet using various deep networks. These findings support learned gradient estimates as a useful alternative to fixed heuristics in the tested settings. The approach alleviates the training obstacle posed by non-differentiability and supports end-to-end optimization; it does not make the discrete quantization operation itself differentiable.
neurips-2019-metaquant-learning-to-quant.tldr: MetaQuant jointly trains a meta network to supply useful weight-update gradients through non-differentiable quantization.

paragraphs: Agents acting without centralized control can struggle to coordinate because each has only partial information. This paper uses common knowledge: information on which agents can independently agree. Such knowledge can arise when agents reconstruct parts of one another’s observations, providing a shared basis for coordinated decisions without centralized execution.

MACKRL learns a hierarchical policy tree through a stochastic actor-critic algorithm. Higher levels coordinate groups using their common knowledge. They can also delegate decisions to smaller subgroups, which may share richer information. This hierarchy lets the policy vary the scope of coordination according to the knowledge available among the participating agents.

The entire tree supports decentralized execution. Its lowest level contains independent policies for individual agents, so independently learned decentralized behavior is included as a special case. Experiments on a stochastic matrix game and StarCraft II unit micromanagement demonstrate superior performance through exploiting common knowledge. The findings show how shared information can support complex coordination even when agents must execute their policies separately.
neurips-2019-multi-agent-common-knowledg.tldr: MACKRL learns a hierarchy of policies that uses common knowledge to coordinate groups while preserving fully decentralized execution.

paragraphs: Hyperbolic embeddings can represent hierarchical data accurately using compact representations. Knowledge graphs present an additional challenge because different relationships can impose different hierarchies on the same entities. The paper addresses this multiplicity, which the existing hyperbolic models discussed in the abstract do not capture.

MuRP places entities in the Poincaré ball, a model of hyperbolic space, and learns parameters specific to each relationship. It uses Möbius matrix-vector multiplication and Möbius addition to transform entity embeddings. These relation-dependent transformations give the model a way to account for multiple hierarchies while keeping its representations in hyperbolic geometry.

The authors evaluate link prediction on WN18RR, a hierarchical knowledge graph. Their Poincaré embeddings outperform both a Euclidean counterpart and existing embedding methods, especially when the embedding dimension is small. The finding supports the combination of hyperbolic geometry and relation-specific transformations for this task. The emphasis on lower dimensionality matters because the model obtains strong reported results with relatively compact entity representations.
neurips-2019-multi-relational-poincare-g.tldr: MuRP uses relation-specific transformations in hyperbolic space to represent multiple hierarchies and improve compact knowledge-graph embeddings.

paragraphs: The paper extends learning from contradictions, also called Universum learning, to classification problems with multiple classes. It introduces a multiclass Universum support vector machine, or MU-SVM. The central idea is to make contradiction information part of the learning formulation and examine whether it improves on a standard multiclass SVM.

The theoretical analysis derives the Natarajan dimension, a measure used to characterize sample requirements for multiclass learning. Through this analysis, the authors show lower sample complexity for MU-SVM than for the ordinary multiclass formulation. They also derive an analytic span bound for model selection, providing a way to choose models with less computation than standard resampling procedures.

The reported model-selection computation is approximately two to four times faster than resampling. Across several real-world datasets, the authors report test-accuracy improvements exceeding 20% compared with multiclass SVM. They additionally use histograms of projections to examine the method’s behavior. Together, these contributions combine a sample-complexity argument, a more efficient model-selection tool, and empirical evidence for incorporating contradictions into multiclass learning.
neurips-2019-multiclass-learning-from-co.tldr: MU-SVM incorporates contradictions into multiclass learning, with lower theoretical sample complexity and reported gains in accuracy and model-selection speed.

paragraphs: LSTMs can require substantial memory and computation, making weight quantization an attractive compression strategy. Yet quantization methods that compress weights often produce inferior results when applied to these networks. This paper investigates the training dynamics behind that performance loss and considers normalization as a way to address it.

The theoretical analysis shows that quantization makes exploding gradients more severe, particularly for large LSTM weight matrices. Exploding gradients create excessively large training signals, making weight updates difficult to control. The authors then show that commonly used weight, layer, and batch normalization schemes can help stabilize gradient magnitudes when training quantized LSTMs.

In the reported experiments, normalized quantized LSTMs perform significantly better than their unnormalized counterparts. They also achieve performance comparable to full-precision LSTMs while using much smaller models. The contribution links a specific theoretical explanation for training difficulty to a practical intervention. The results indicate that managing gradient behavior can preserve much of an LSTM’s predictive performance while retaining the size benefits of quantized weights.
neurips-2019-normalization-helps-trainin.tldr: Normalization stabilizes gradients in quantized LSTMs, enabling much smaller models with performance comparable to full-precision networks in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: The paper explores how to combine information stored in the learned representations of autoencoders. Its models mix attributes from multiple inputs and turn the combined representation into a resynthesized output. An adversarial discriminator judges whether outputs are real or synthesized, giving the mixing system a training objective tied to the realism of its results.

The authors also study this architecture for semi-supervised learning. In that setting, they learn a mixing function that produces either interpolations between hidden states or masked combinations of latent representations. The combinations are trained to remain consistent with a specified class label, linking representation mixing to the class information available during learning.

The reported evidence includes both quantitative results and qualitative examples. The authors present these as support for a promising research direction, rather than as a broad claim of superiority. The approach matters because it treats combining learned representations as a trainable operation, with adversarial realism and class consistency shaping what kinds of combinations the model produces.
neurips-2019-on-adversarial-mixup-resynt.tldr: The paper explores learned mixing of autoencoder representations to produce realistic outputs and class-consistent combinations for semi-supervised learning.

paragraphs: Park is a research platform for applying reinforcement learning to computer-system optimization. The paper starts from the observation that systems problems differ in important ways from familiar reinforcement-learning settings such as games. It discusses those distinctive challenges and seeks to make systems research more accessible to machine-learning researchers.

The platform brings together 12 real-world optimization problems centered on computer systems. Each uses a common interface, giving researchers a consistent way to interact with otherwise different tasks. Park is also open and extensible, so its contribution includes a framework for experimentation beyond an individual learning algorithm or a single optimization problem.

The authors evaluate existing reinforcement-learning approaches across the 12 problems and identify directions for future work. This evaluation provides a picture of how available approaches perform within the platform’s collection of tasks. The paper’s main contribution is therefore shared experimental infrastructure and an accompanying assessment, creating a practical setting for studying the particular demands of reinforcement learning in computer systems.
neurips-2019-park-an-open-platform-for-l.tldr: Park provides a common, extensible interface to 12 computer-system optimization problems for reinforcement-learning research.

paragraphs: Temporal-difference learning updates value estimates using information from other state-action pairs. This paper asks how uncertainty about those values should move through the same learning process. It develops a Bayesian framework that represents uncertainty with approximate posterior distributions, keeping track of more than a single estimated value.

The framework uses Wasserstein barycenters to propagate these distributions across state-action pairs. These provide a way to combine distributions according to Wasserstein geometry. The resulting algorithm, Wasserstein Q-Learning, is first developed for tabular problems and then extended to continuous domains. The central contribution is a structured rule for carrying uncertainty through value learning.

For a slight variation of the algorithm, the authors prove desirable theoretical properties under mild assumptions in the tabular setting. Experiments on finite problems demonstrate effectiveness against several reinforcement-learning algorithms, including methods designed for exploration. The paper also provides preliminary Atari results. The theory and experiments have distinct scopes: the stated guarantees concern the tabular variant, while the broader-domain results supply empirical evidence.
neurips-2019-propagating-uncertainty-in-.tldr: Wasserstein Q-Learning propagates Bayesian value uncertainty using Wasserstein barycenters, with tabular theoretical results and empirical exploration benefits.

paragraphs: Optimal transport becomes difficult in high dimensions. Projecting distributions into smaller spaces makes computation easier, but a transport map learned there only describes movement within that projection. The paper addresses how to recover a useful map between the original distributions, rather than stopping at a distance or map in reduced dimensions.

The authors propose two methods that extend a map optimal on a subspace into one that is nearly optimal in the full space. They show that the best transport plan constrained to take these subspace detours generalizes Knothe-Rosenblatt transport. This connects the construction to an established transport framework while retaining the subspace as an intermediate step.

For Gaussian measures, the resulting plans have explicit formulations. The paper also gives an algorithm for choosing optimal mediating subspaces for Gaussian pairs and studies when prior information can guide that choice. Applications include semantic mediation between elliptic word embeddings and domain adaptation with Gaussian mixture models. The approach makes low-dimensional transport useful for constructing maps in the original space.
neurips-2019-subspace-detours-building-t.tldr: Subspace detours extend transport maps from low-dimensional projections into nearly optimal maps between the original distributions.

paragraphs: The paper studies whether profile maximum likelihood, or PML, can serve as one statistical approach across distribution estimation, property estimation, and hypothesis testing. Its main contribution is a collection of sample-efficiency guarantees, showing that the same approach achieves optimal or near-optimal requirements across a wide range of tasks.

For sorted-distribution estimation under l1 distance, PML achieves optimal sample complexity of order k/(ε² log k). For a broad class of additive properties, its plug-in estimator uses four times the best estimator’s sample size to obtain roughly twice the error with exponentially higher confidence. Rényi entropy results distinguish integer orders above one, where sample complexity is optimal, from non-integer orders above three quarters, where the stated bounds improve on prior results.

For identity testing, a PML-based method is optimal up to logarithmic factors in alphabet size. An estimator based on PML also empirically outperforms Good-Turing for actual-distribution estimation. Most theoretical results extend, with minor changes, to a near-linear-time variant. These distinctions matter: exact optimality, approximate optimality, and empirical improvement apply to different claims.
neurips-2019-the-broad-optimality-of-pro.tldr: Profile maximum likelihood provides a unified approach with optimal or near-optimal sample requirements across many estimation and testing tasks.

paragraphs: A common variational-autoencoder setup models image pixels with a Bernoulli likelihood. The paper identifies a mismatch in this practice: a Bernoulli variable takes only the values zero and one, while the pixel data being modeled can take any value between them. The authors argue that this discrepancy materially changes the model’s behavior.

They introduce and fully characterize the continuous Bernoulli, a single-parameter probability distribution supported on the entire interval from zero to one. This provides a likelihood whose allowed values match the continuous pixel data in question. The contribution directly addresses the probabilistic model used by the VAE, rather than treating the support mismatch as an inconsequential implementation detail.

The authors report meaningful improvements across multiple datasets and evaluation metrics, including sharper generated images. Their analysis finds both qualitative and quantitative consequences from correcting the likelihood. These results show that choosing a distribution compatible with the observed data can have practical effects on VAE performance, and they motivate investigation of a broader class of effective VAE models.
neurips-2019-the-continuous-bernoulli-fi.tldr: The continuous Bernoulli corrects a mismatch between continuous pixel values and Bernoulli likelihoods, improving reported VAE performance.

paragraphs: Variational Bayes offers scalable posterior inference by using an approximating family of distributions. Much of its theoretical support assumes that the statistical model is correctly specified. This paper examines the more realistic possibility that the chosen model cannot exactly represent the true process generating the data.

The authors establish asymptotic normality of the variational posterior and its centering at the model value closest to the true distribution in Kullback-Leibler divergence. The posterior mean also centers at that value and is asymptotically normal. These results extend the variational Bernstein–von Mises theorem to misspecified models, explaining the limiting behavior of inference when the model itself is imperfect.

A consequence is that model misspecification error dominates variational approximation error in the posterior predictive distributions covered by the analysis. This helps explain why variational Bayes can predict comparably to MCMC despite its approximation. The paper illustrates three forms of misspecification, including incorrect dispersion and latent dimensionality, and provides two simulation studies. The asymptotic results do not assert identical finite-sample behavior for all models.
neurips-2019-variational-bayes-under-mod.tldr: The paper characterizes variational Bayes under misspecified models and explains how model error can dominate predictive approximation error.

paragraphs: A calibrated probability should reflect how often the corresponding prediction is correct. The paper finds that popular post-processing methods, including Platt and temperature scaling, are less calibrated than reported and that existing assessment techniques cannot measure their remaining miscalibration. Histogram binning offers measurable error but requires more samples.

The proposed scaling-binning calibrator combines a fitted parametric function with binning of its outputs. The fitted function serves as a baseline for reducing variance, while binning supplies the calibration guarantee. For B distinct output probabilities and target accuracy ε, the method requires O(1/ε² + B) samples, compared with O(B/ε²) for histogram binning. This reduces the sample burden associated with obtaining verifiable calibration.

The authors also analyze an alternative calibration-error estimator from meteorology, proving a requirement of O(√B) samples instead of O(B). Experiments on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet report 35% lower calibration error than histogram binning, together with guarantees on true calibration unavailable from the scaling methods considered. The paper therefore improves both recalibration and the ability to assess it.
neurips-2019-verified-uncertainty-calibr.tldr: Scaling-binning combines sample-efficient recalibration with verifiable guarantees, while an improved estimator reduces the data needed to assess calibration error.

paragraphs: Maximizing mutual information is a common objective for learning representations without labels. The paper identifies a statistical obstacle: obtaining a tight lower bound requires a sample size exponential in the mutual information. In high-information prediction settings, this can encourage overfitting and representations that capture only some relevant factors of variation.

The authors empirically demonstrate incomplete representations on both designed and real-world tasks. They then introduce the Wasserstein dependency measure, replacing the KL-divergence-based comparison in the mutual-information estimator with Wasserstein distance. The motivation is to change the dependency objective so that learning can retain a more complete account of the information relevant to downstream tasks.

A practical approximation uses Lipschitz-constraint techniques drawn from GAN research. The resulting approach substantially improves results on tasks where incomplete representations are a major challenge. These findings support the proposed alternative in the evaluated settings and connect its motivation to a concrete sample-complexity problem. The claim concerns tight mutual-information lower bounds and the affected learning approaches, rather than every possible use of mutual information.
neurips-2019-wasserstein-dependency-meas.tldr: A Wasserstein-based dependency objective learns more complete representations in tasks where mutual-information estimation suffers from severe sample demands.
